title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
section: Let the GPT provide aesthetic suggestions
text:
Let the GPT provide aesthetic suggestions
Besides schoolwork, I have been working on editing my birthday portraits diligently, and suddenly became curious about how an LLM could help. Photo editing requires emotional perception and a keen aesthetic sense. Would a connection-based model like GPT be capable of such a task?
To test its ability, I selected three photos, each with a slightly different color tone. I wrote the following prompt:

These are some portraits I took during my birthday. You are an experienced photographer who has strong expertise and a good sense of aesthetic judgment. Please give me detailed suggestions on how to edit or do color adjustment on these raw photos to enhance them and make them more appealing and artistic. Please also explain the rationales behind your suggestions.

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
text:
A number-extensive response
GPT 5’s thinking mode produced a response that seems to be really comprehensive. It startw with a global look to unify the set of the three photos, and identify the goal should be “dreamy, romantic ‘buttery yellow’ palettee.” Based on this goal, he gave out the exact statistics on the references:
**White balance**
*Outdoor shots*: push a touch warmer and magenta to counter green foliage and blue skylight on skin. Temp +300 to +600K, Tint +5 to +12.
*Indoor window shot*: neutral-warm but not orange. Temp –100 to +150K from camera, Tint +3 to +7.

**Tone Curve**
Subtle S-curve*:Lift shadows slightly (point curve floor to ~4–6).Pull mid-highlight just a hair up. Optionally lift extreme highlights minimally to keep porcelain statue detail.

**Presence**
*Texture*: –5 to –15 on skin (via mask), +5 to +10 on hair/eyes/dress stitching.
*Clarity*: 0 to +8 overall; avoid high clarity on skin.
*Dehaze*: –2 to +3 only; too much looks crunchy.
After this unified overview, it then provided specific “recipes” for each photo, with extensive numbers and metrices just like above. Finally, it listed export suggestions to preserve the final look, which I thought was a nice, thoughtful touch. To conclude, it invited more personalized adjustments, likely a learned behavior from its training process to encourage further interaction.

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
text:
The final product
By this point, however, I was already overwhelmed by the sheer volume of numbers. In a natural interaction with a human photographer, they would never recite such specific statistics right away. They would show you the effects visually, because human senses don’t directly process numbers in such an aesthetic and perceptual task. So, I asked it to apply these settings directly to the photos.
A comoparison of edited versions…




Original on the left, modified on the right







Original on the left, modified on the right







Original on the left, modified on the right



Well, maybe machines have their own taste, but I will not be taking photo editing advice from GPT5 again.

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
text:
A different approach than humans
The process of editing a photo is often a trial-and-error process for human. Even an experienced editor will experiment with different settings, constantly evaluating and comparing the results, and then continuously adjusting based on their experience and intuition. The exact numbers given by the LLM can be a helpful initial starting point, but lacking the ability for holistic, emotional judgment, it can only provide solutions based on its training data and wait for a human’s instructions to make iterative adjustments.

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
text:
Final thoughts
This also makes me wonder—since all its solutions are derived from associative data, can it only produce “average” artwork? Can it create novel and bold aesthetics through genuine experimentation? And how might different prompting strategies affect that outcome?

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
text: Interview with an LLM

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
text:
Gemini as my potential user
My Product Management course tasked us with conducting a User Empathy Interview with ChatGPT. Specifically, we had to conceive a product, identify potential user personas, design interview questions to understand user needs and behaviors, and then have the LLM role-play the persona while we conducted the interview.
I ultimately chose the Gemini 2.5 Pro model, believing it can “mimic” human communicative behaviors and langauge better than other models, because Google as a company has got massive real user data to train their models.
My product is an AI-powered learning tool aimed at enhancing class engagement. I identified my first potential user persona as a high school student:

You are a 14-year-old high school student in a US public high school, who is afraid of in-class discussion because she either feels having nothing to say about the content, or the discussion focus was often irrelevant to her thoughts and she couldn’t catch up. From now, I will be conducting a user interview with you regarding an education product.

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
text:
An compelling but unatural act
Gemini immediately adopted the persona, even including paralanguage in the form of action annotations:

(adjusts in my chair, pulls the sleeves of my hoodie over my hands) Oh, okay. Hi. Um, yeah, I’m ready whenever you are. Is it okay if I’m, like, a little nervous? I’m not really used to stuff like this. (looks around the room for a second) So… you’re just gonna ask me questions about school and stuff? Okay. Cool. Yeah, ask away, I guess.

My initial instinct was to tell Gemini to omit the actions, but I recalled my professor’s point that in-person interviews offer additional insights from non-verbal cues. Curious about this simulated multimodal communication, I decided to continue:

Can you walk me through the last time you had a class discussion about an article you had to read or a video you had to watch? What was that experience like for you?

“Her” response was remarkably detailed:

Okay, um, yeah. Let’s see… the last time was probably on Tuesday, in my English class. We have Ms. Davis. We had to read this really short, kinda creepy story called “The Lottery” for homework the night before. I read it, and I thought it was… wow, like, really messed up. So…(Anotehr 300 words of vivid description here)…I just sat there and listened. It feels… I dunno, frustrating? You feel really small and kinda stupid, even when you did the reading and you think you understand it. My heart just beats really fast the whole time, hoping she doesn’t call on me.

It’s unusual for a real human to provide such a structured and detailed recollection of an experience. Human memories are often disorganized, emotionally charged, and filled with subjective highlights. This response, while compelling, felt almost too logical and rich to be a genuine human recall. If it’s an interrogation of suspect, such a coherent narrative would be seen as rehearsed.



A struggling student

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
section: My own communicative strategy also changed with an LLM
text:
My own communicative strategy also changed with an LLM
I also identified the flaws in my own quesioning.I asked too many questions at once, assuming the LLM could address them all in a single reply. This is a common pitfall when shifting from human to AI interaction, as humans typically process and respond to questions sequentially within a shorter turn-taking framework:

I understand that. How do your group discussions typically start? When a teacher provides a specific question to start your group’s conversation, what makes a question effective or ineffective for you personally? Can you remember an example of a prompt that made it easy to talk?

As expected, it did answer all questions together. Unexpectedly, it culminated in a sudden ending:

*(Looks at the clock on the wall, getting a little antsy) Okay, so when we get into our little groups, there’s usually this super awkward moment of silence after we move the desks. Everyone just kinda looks at each other, and then someone will finally be like…(Another 400 words of vivid description here) It didn’t feel like I was going to get a bad grade if my opinion was “wrong.” I talked a lot in that discussion. (BRRRRRING!) Oh, that’s the final bell. I have to run or I’ll miss my bus. Um, it was nice talking to you. I hope that was helpful. Bye! (quickly gathers my stuff and heads for the door)

I had two more questions prepared, but didn’t get a chance to ask – “she” had to leave! This unexpected conclusion, a simulated abrupt exit, felt as chaotic and unpredictable as a real-life interview. I found this “out-of-control” situation quite amusing.



She left

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
section: LLMs as useful tools to conduct user interviews
text:
LLMs as useful tools to conduct user interviews
In conclusion, despite some of the conversational structures feeling unnatural, interviewing an LLM proved to be a surprisingly helpful way to conduct user research. They are much more “knowledgeable” and elaborative than a human subject, and thus can provide richer details and insights for the product, as reported in my homework:

Key insights & informed product design from User A:


Prioritize Humanities Subjects: Initial product development should focus on discussion-heavy subjects like English and History. These fields present a clear opportunity, as students often find it challenging to participate in discussions that require subjective interpretation and personal reflection.


Generate Accessible Prompts: The AI product’s core function should be to generate opening discussion prompts that are personal, opinion-based, and directly relevant to students’ lived experiences. To encourage participation, the system must prioritize accessible questions over abstract, academic language that can intimidate hesitant speakers.

title: A Picture Worth 10x Fewer Tokens?
text:
AI reads through images
When I saw DeepSeek released DeepSeek-OCR as a small 3-billion-parameter model, I was wondering why a team of top-tier AI talent would spend their energy on OCR (Optical Character Recognition), which has been a “solved” problem for ages? But it turned out the depth iscertainly hidden from the average eye.

title: A Picture Worth 10x Fewer Tokens?
section: Challenging AI’s Unit of Cost: The Token
text:
Challenging AI’s Unit of Cost: The Token
To understand, we need a quick refresher on the AI’s “unit of payment”: the Token. You can think of the Token as the basic “food” or computational cost for the AI. One Chinese character is about 1–2 Tokens, and an English word might be 1–3. Every Token processed costs money, slows down speed, and consumes resources. Therefore, the core challenge of the AI era is how to convey maximum information with minimum Token count.
We often say, “A picture is worth a thousand words,” but DeepSeek-OCR decided to prove it with hard data. They aren’t building a better scanner but investigating the question: How much effort does AI save by “looking at a picture” versus “reading text”?

title: A Picture Worth 10x Fewer Tokens?
text:
The 10x Compression Data
Through their experiments, they discovered an efficiency gap: A document containing roughly 1,000 text tokens for text processing, but when processed by visual comprehension it requires only 100 visual Tokens, while achieving 97% accuracy. This is a 10x compression with virtually no information loss. Even pushing the compression ratio to 20x, accuracy remains at about 60%, which is impressive. Just as the human brain has different processing channels (sound for music, sight for charts), AI models found that encoding and compressing text-heavy documents through a visual model is far more efficient than traditional text-only processing.

title: A Picture Worth 10x Fewer Tokens?
section: The Core Secret: DeepEncoder’s Three-Step Process
text:
The Core Secret: DeepEncoder’s Three-Step Process
This massive efficiency gain is thanks to a custom-designed encoder called the DeepEncoder. Its workflow is systematic and effective:

Window Attention (Local Observation): First, the DeepEncoder scans the content piece by piece, similar to the human eye.
Compression Module (Information Distillation): It then compresses the local information by 16x, retaining only key features.
Global Attention (Core Extraction): Finally, it extracts the truly useful core knowledge, ensuring full comprehension.

The results speak for themselves. A highly-rated OCR model like MinerU2.0 uses over 6,000 Tokens to process one page. DeepSeek-OCR uses less than 800 Tokens and achieves superior results.

title: A Picture Worth 10x Fewer Tokens?
text:
Real-World Utility and Industry Impact
The practical value of this model can be immense. A single A100 GPU can process 200,000 document pages per day. This means massive, low-cost conversion of PDF documents into structured data for training larger language models. DeepSeek can process several times the amount of data compared to others using the same compute resources.
Former OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy reflected this disruptive potential, commenting on X: “Maybe it is more reasonable that all inputs to LLMs should be images. Even if you have pure text input, you should render it first, and then input it.”
I would say this work is an exploration into the essence of AI information processing. DeepSeek shows us that the future of AI is not defined by infinite computing power, but by smarter encoding.

title: Beyond the ‘Overall’ Score: AI’s Intersectional Blind Spot
text:
Caution
In the book Unmasking AI, the author connects a core concept in legal theory—intersectionality—to a deep flaw in machine learning. The book draws on the work of legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw to explain “multi-axis discrimination” and shows how AI risks repeating the exact same mistakes.

title: Beyond the ‘Overall’ Score: AI’s Intersectional Blind Spot
text:
What is Multi-Axis Discrimination?
Coined by Crenshaw, intersectionality describes how individuals can face multiple, overlapping forms of discrimination, like racism and sexism. These factors don’t exist in isolation; they can combine to create unique forms of disadvantage. When systems only look for “racism” or “sexism” (a single axis), they often completely miss the compound discrimination faced by those at the intersection, such as women of color. The book provides a stark hiring example: A company “proves” it isn’t racist by pointing to the Black men it hired, and “proves” it isn’t sexist by pointing to the white women it hired. By looking at race and gender separately, the system meets the law. But it completely overlooks the Black women, Asian women, or other women of color who are systematically excluded. If they don’t get hired, they would have no legal basis to rederess.

title: Beyond the ‘Overall’ Score: AI’s Intersectional Blind Spot
section: The AI Connection: The Tyranny of the Single Metric
text:
The AI Connection: The Tyranny of the Single Metric
This is where the author connects this legal blind spot to machine learning. AI models are often judged by a single, “overall” performance metric, like “95% accuracy” in a predictive task. But this single number is just like the company’s flawed hiring defense. It hides who the model is failing. Let’s apply this to a facial recognition system. An “overall accuracy” of 95% might break down like this: - Performance on white men: 99.8% - Performance on white women: 97% - Performance on Black men: 85% - Performance on Black women: 70%
The “overall” score looks great only because it’s weighted by high performance on the dominant groups. It masks the system’s dangerous failures at the intersections. The system isn’t “95% accurate”; it’s a system that works for some and fails, often harmfully, for others.



Quote from Kimberlé Crenshaw

title: Beyond the ‘Overall’ Score: AI’s Intersectional Blind Spot
text:
The Impact on Educational Equity
This reminded me of a machine learning project in education that I did. The “single metric” problem has dangerous and practical implications for education equity, where AI is increasingly used to make high-stakes decisions.
Schools already lean heavily on single metrics: GPA, standardized test scores, “on track” flags in student dashboards. As AI tools enter classrooms—adaptive learning platforms, early-warning systems, automated essay scoring, “at-risk” prediction models—they often replicate that same logic in code. A model might boast “92% accuracy in predicting who will pass the course,” but that number can obscure which students it systematically gets wrong.
Imagine a district using an AI system to identify students who need extra support. The model performs well “on average,” but breaks down like this: - High accuracy for white, middle-class students - Lower accuracy for multilingual learners - Even worse accuracy for, say, recently immigrated girls of color in under-resourced schools
On paper, the system looks like a success. In practice, it might consistently under-flag some groups (denying them needed support) or over-flag them (subjecting them to extra surveillance, remediation, or stigma). Just as in the hiring example, the district can point to data showing “we support girls” and “we support students of color” in aggregate—while missing those at the intersection who are misclassified, misunderstood, or left behind.

title: Beyond the ‘Overall’ Score: AI’s Intersectional Blind Spot
text:
The Path Forward
For educators and designers, the lesson is clear: it’s not enough to ask, “Does this AI work for students?” We have to ask, “For which students, under what conditions, and at what intersections of race, gender, language, disability, and class?” That means disaggregating performance metrics, involving students and families from marginalized groups in the design process, and treating “overall success” as a starting point, not a finish line.
If we don’t, AI in education risks becoming just another polished dashboard that tells a comforting story about improvement—while quietly reproducing the same old patterns of inequity, now with the authority of an algorithm behind them.

title: When should we consider using role-playing prompting?
text:
children’s pretend play
My interview with Gemini last time was fun, feeling much like a childhood pretend play. The language it adopted as a high schooler felt authentic, and its subsequent role as a teacher demonstrated a truly “pedagogical” voice and mannerisms. This made me wonder: Beyond merely affecting tone, does assigning a specific persona to an LLM truly enhance its task performance? And if so, in what ways?
Conducting a thorough experiment myself would be challenging, so I turned to the resesarch papers for a comprehensive and validated answer. Here’s what I found:

title: When should we consider using role-playing prompting?
section: Assigning a persona to an LLM can have a multifaceted impact
text:
Assigning a persona to an LLM can have a multifaceted impact
On Reasoning Ability:

Benefits: A 2023 study found that role-play prompting can act as an implicit, as well as a better “Chain-of-Thought” (CoT) trigger than CoT instruction alone. It guides the model to break down complex problems into a series of intermediate reasoning steps, which can lead to more accurate and logical conclusions (Kong et al., 2023). Other work shows role-play can boost task reasoning (e.g., arithmetic/commonsense) by helping the model adopt a problem-solving stance (Zhao, et al., 2024). For example, embodying a “math teacher” persona encourages the LLM to adopt a more structured and explanatory approach to solving problems (Kong et al., 2023).




Reasoning as a math teacher



Caveats: However, the introduction of personas has risks. Research has shown that while role-playing can improve reasoning, it can also amplify inherent biases present in the training data. Multiple studies report that role-play can amplify bias, toxicity, and unsafe outputs, especially when personas encode social attributes such as occupation, gender, race or religion (Shen et al., 2024).

On Factual Accuracy:

While the results are mixed (sometimes task accuracy improves due to enhanced reasoning), larger studies and meta-analyses generally indicate that adding a persona usually does not improve factual accuracy and can even slightly diminish it on average (Zheng et al., 2024). The effects of personas are also highly unpredictable; the same role might assist on one item but hinder another, and simple strategies for selecting “the best role” perform almost randomly.
A Particular Caveat: A 2024 study investigated how role-playing different social identities affects ChatGPT’s ability to classify misinformation. The findings were stark: including social identities in prompts significantly reduced average detection accuracy from 68.1% (with no identity) to as low as 19.2% (with a political identity). This suggests that when a model adopts a persona with inherent biases or worldviews, its capacity to objectively evaluate information for accuracy can be severely compromised (Harris, 2024).

title: When should we consider using role-playing prompting?
section: Do the effects differ cross domains?
text:
Do the effects differ cross domains?
In specialized fields, context matters. For instance, in medicine, assigning an expert persona can improve the accuracy and comprehensiveness of patient-facing information (Li et al., 2024).
Furthermore, a modeling approach called REGA (Wang et al., 2024) shows that when models are fine-tuned using role prompts in fields like law, medicine, or finance, and then used with a generalist role, their performance improves across these domains compared to baselines. This highlights a more integrated training strategy — not a user-level prompt though(Wang et al., 2024).



LLM playing a medicine specialist

title: When should we consider using role-playing prompting?
text:
A short conclusion
It appear that, in general, role-play prompting does not lead to better task outcomes/accuracy. Even if it does, it’s typically through improved domain-structured reasoning (e.g., clinical reasoning prompts), or by adopting a specific framework of thinking and reasoning in the particular field. But be careful — this could also lead to enhanced bias embedded in the training data.
When to Consider Using Role-Play Prompting

When You Need Structured, Domain-Specific Reasoning: As mentioned, a relevant persona can better guide the model to adopt a particular domain-specific reasoning framework, accessing and applying specialized knowledge.
When Tasks Are Subjective, Personal, or Creative: Persona prompts truly excel in interpretive or creative tasks where a particular viewpoint, communication style, or emotional resonance is desired.

Avoid Role-Play Prompting

When Seeking Factual Information: Introducing a persona can reduce factual accuracy, making it less suitable for tasks requiring strict objectivity(we shouldn’t rely on LLMs for exact factual knowledge anyways).
When Concerned About Bias: If the output’s fairness, neutrality, or safety is paramount, assigning a persona, especially one with social attributes, risks amplifying problematic elements from the training data.


References


Harris, J. K. (2024). Evaluating the influence of role-playing prompts on ChatGPT’s misinformation detection accuracy: Quantitative study. JMIR Infodemiology. Advance online publication.


Kong, A., Zhao, S., Chen, H., Li, Q., Qin, Y., Sun, R., … & Dong, X. (2023). Better zero-shot reasoning with role-play prompting. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.07702


Pei, J., Tang, R., & Fu, K. W. (2024). When “a helpful assistant” is not really helpful: Personas in system prompts do not improve performances of large language models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10054


Shen, Y., et al. (2024). Role-play paradox in large language models: Reasoning performance gains and ethical dilemmas. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08352


Wang, R., Mi, F., Chen, Y., Xue, B., Wang, H., Zhu, Q., … & Xu, R. (2024). Role prompting guided domain adaptation with general capability preserve for large language models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02756


Zhao, J., et al. (2024). Role-play paradox in large language models: Reasoning performance gains and ethical dilemmas. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13979


Zheng, M., Pei, J., Logeswaran, L., Lee, M., & Jurgens, D. (2024, November). When “a helpful assistant” is not really helpful: Personas in system prompts do not improve performances of large language models. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024 (pp. 15126–15154). Association for Computational Linguistics.

title: Stop Asking AI to ‘Do Things’ — Ask It to Teach You Instead
text:
Tool v.s. Tutoring Modes
In the rush to integrate AI into daily workflows, many users default to treating it like a high-tech vending machine: input a request, get an output. This “Tool-mode” approach—prompts like “Write this email for me”—prioritizes speed and automation, echoing an industrial-era focus on efficiency over understanding.
But data from OpenAI’s report, How People Use ChatGPT, challenges this mindset. Analyzing over a million conversations, the study reveals that “Asking” interactions (seeking advice, clarification, or guidance) account for 49% of messages, outpacing “Doing” (task execution) at 40%, with “Expressing” (sharing views or feelings) at 11%. Notably, Asking is growing faster, and these conversations consistently earn higher satisfaction ratings from users—both via automated classifiers and direct feedback. This shift suggests AI’s true value lies not in replacing human effort, but in enhancing it through mentorship.

title: Stop Asking AI to ‘Do Things’ — Ask It to Teach You Instead
section: Tool-Mode vs. Mentor-Mode: Why the Distinction Matters
text:
Tool-Mode vs. Mentor-Mode: Why the Distinction Matters
At its core, the difference boils down to intent and outcome. Consider these paired prompts: Tool-mode:”Write an email to my boss requesting a project extension.”
Mentor-mode: “How should I structure an email to my boss requesting a project extension? What key elements—like tone, evidence, and timing—should I consider to make it persuasive?”
From the report, about 10% of all messages involve tutoring or teaching, a subset of Practical Guidance (the top category at 29%). This indicates users are intuitively seeking AI as a coach for skill-building, not just output generation.



More Asking than Doing

title: Stop Asking AI to ‘Do Things’ — Ask It to Teach You Instead
text:
The Psychological Edge of Mentor-Mode
Why do users report greater satisfaction with advisory interactions? Drawing from learning science:

Boosted Agency and Ownership: Tool-mode entirely outsources cognitive labor. Mentor-mode, conversely, supports the user’s decision-making, shifting the user’s role from passive “operator” to active “author” who maintains control over the final outcome.
Reducing Cognitive Uncertainty: Many queries stem from ambiguity, not laziness. Mentor-mode provides mental models for navigating complexity, like decision trees or pros/cons lists, which reduce anxiety and build confidence.
Supporting Judgment in Real-World Skills: Expertise in areas like communication or problem-solving requires adaptive thinking under constraints. Mentor-mode trains this by explaining trade-offs, mirroring apprenticeship models where novices learn through guided practice.

Empirically, the report shows Asking messages have a higher “good-to-bad” quality ratio, likely because they create iterative, engaging dialogues that feel more collaborative.

title: Stop Asking AI to ‘Do Things’ — Ask It to Teach You Instead
section: EdTech’s Call to Action: Design for Coaching, Not Just Completion
text:
EdTech’s Call to Action: Design for Coaching, Not Just Completion
For EdTech developers, this data demands a pivot from automation tools to adaptive mentors. The goal? Shift users from consumers of content to builders of competence.
Core Design Principle: Prioritize processes that generate thinking, not just artifacts.
Here are some practical applications, grounded in the report’s findings on education-related use (e.g., tutoring at 10% of messages) and higher-educated users’ preference for Asking:

Question-first UX: before drafting, the system asks 3 clarifying questions that a good teacher would ask.
Reasoning transparency: short “why this works” bullets.
Practice loops: “Want to try a version in your voice? I’ll help refine.” Metacognitive prompts: “What outcome matters most: speed, relationship, credibility, or accuracy?”

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs
section: My LLMs sometimes know more about me than I do
text:
My LLMs sometimes know more about me than I do
It’s the beginning of another beautiful semester — and according to the syllabus of my communication course, we are required to pick a book from a list of seven on the topic of AI to read throughout the academic term.
Usually, I would let my large language model introduce each book to me to get a snapshot and then make a judgment myself. This time, I decided to take it a step further and treat the interaction as a small communicative experiment. I would ask the LLM to act as a consultant and actively suggest the best options for me.
This should be a reasonable task for an LLM: I’ve been using this particular model mainly for school and work since 2023, so our interaction history forms a rich data of my academic and intellectual interests. Therefore, it should be able to generate tailored suggestions. However,I decided to make my intention clear in the ask, because I don’t assume it will automatically take my background into account, which a human would probably do:




Image



Here, instead of merely paraphrasing the assignment, I included the full text from the syllabus. From a pragmatics perspective, this provides the LLM with maximum context for the current exchange (Shhh, not because I was too lazy).
After 42 seconds, the model returned a long response structured in a very deliberate way: * An opening comment on the assignment. * His top 3 picks with rationales.


 ***


A parting line, then a short introduction for each book.
Another parting line, then ideas for how the books could be incorporated into my existing work.



 ***


A final parting line, the suggested ranking list
Tips for the assignment and, finally, a follow-up question to invite more interaction.



 ***

The response was comprehensive, seemingly designed to anticipate and address all my potential questions.

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs
section: Is unnecessarily long for a natural human interaction
text:
Is unnecessarily long for a natural human interaction
While I found the response useful, it was excessively lengthy, especially considering the computational energy LLMs consume. I often have the sense that they favor exhaustiveness over the brevity we often value in human conversation, because talking is energy-consuming.

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs
section: But here are the things I truly appreciated:
text:
But here are the things I truly appreciated:

It provided a ready-to-use ranked list. The LLM correctly parsed the prompt’s explicit instructions (“rank your preferences”) and structured its primary output to meet that specific need.
It provided rationales connecting to my past work, which allowed me to critically evaluate the rationales and re-weigh my current prioritization.
It suggested practical applications. The ideas for incorporating the book’s content into my other projects were genuinely insightful.

Interestingly, this final point highlights a key difference between human and AI communication. It’s difficult to imagine a human expert spontaneously generating such a detailed list of potential operational connections of each book with my past experience in a casual conversation. The tips for class would also be cognitively exausive to provide. While the cognitive load requried for these content would be too high for a human talker, they are easy-peasy for a LLM.

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs
text:
Different mental manipulation mechanisms
So, although the tones and expressions look humane, GPT’s very ability to perform this low-cost, high-output analysis in a causal converstion is actually inhuman, or unatural. It doesn’t rely on the same mental shortcuts as human do. To him, generating these chunks of tasks have no different from the other chunks, computationally.

title: Why We’re All Roleplaying with AI
text:
Role-playing with LLM
For the past two years, the narrative around AI has been dominated by “productivity.” We talk about LLMs as efficient clerks—tools to summarize long threads, debug messy code, or ghostwrite professional emails. But a massive new report from OpenRouter, which analyzed a staggering 100 trillion tokens of real-world usage, just pulled back the curtain on what we’re actually doing with these models.
It turns out, we aren’t just looking for an assistant; we’re looking for a scene partner.
OpenRouter, a platform that lets developers toggle between dozens of different AI models, found that “Roleplay” isn’t just a niche hobby for the internet’s fringes—it is a massive, dominant force. It accounts for over 50% of all open-source model usage as a structured, repeatable genre. People aren’t just asking for facts, we are simulating scenarios and interacting with personas.

title: Why We’re All Roleplaying with AI
text:
The Instinct to Simulate
This dominance of roleplay shouldn’t be dismissed as mere escapism; it aligns with a fundamental human instinct. Developmental psychology tells us that children learn to navigate the world through spontaneous role-play games—“playing house” or “cops and robbers” are essentially low-tech simulations of complex social dynamics.
The OpenRouter report confirms that this behavior doesn’t disappear in adulthood; it just migrates to digital mediums. The data shows that users are treating these models less like chatbots and more like “character engines.” In fact, nearly 60% of roleplay tokens are categorized specifically as “Games/Roleplaying Games,” indicating that users are actively seeking rules, scenarios, and consistent personas rather than just casual conversation. We are seeing a massive, decentralized experiment in “situated learning,” where users are voluntarily engaging in complex simulations to practice social interaction, explore narratives, or experience a different perspective.



Children’s pretend play

title: Why We’re All Roleplaying with AI
section: From “Chatbot” to “Simulator”: The Future of EdTech
text:
From “Chatbot” to “Simulator”: The Future of EdTech
This insight offers a powerful roadmap for the next generation of educational tools. If the market is naturally gravitating toward roleplay, educators should pivot from using AI as an “Oracle” (that simply answers questions) to using AI as a “Simulator.” We can power shifts toward:

Historical Personas: Instead of reading about Lincoln, students could negotiate with a model “locked” into the political constraints of 1862.
Scientific Inquiry: Models could act as “unreliable narrators” or specific scientific phenomena that students must diagnose or debug through conversation.
Career Exploration: High-stakes simulations of job interviews or difficult client negotiations, allowing students to “fail safely” before entering the workforce.

However, the report notes that roleplay currently thrives on open-source models partly because they are “less constrained by content filters.” To make this pedagogically meaningful, we need to design deliberate “scaffolded sandboxes” rather than unconstrained “wild west” environments.

title: Is GPT more empathetic when speaking Chinese?
text:
AI showing empathy
As a bilingual user, I often switch between Chinese and English when interacting with GPT, depending on the task at hand. However, I’ve never paid close attention to any differences in its responses until now. A recent project collecting vocabulary related to body-image anxiety on social media sparked my curiosity: are there cultural trends embedded in these terms? To find out, I prompted ChatGPT with the exact same sentences in both languages. Unexpectedly, it wasn’t just the words that were different—it was the entire way GPT responded.

title: Is GPT more empathetic when speaking Chinese?
text:
Attempt 1: A simple task
My prompts were direct translations of each other:

English: Give me a list of pop-culture slang or terms or abbreviations that are related to body-image anxiety that are popular and widely used on social media, especially among young people. The words can be in any format (nouns, verbs or adjectives).
Chinese: 请给我一份与身材焦虑相关的流行文化俚语、术语或缩写词清单，这些词汇在社交媒体上流行且被广泛使用，尤其是在年轻人当中。这些词可以是任何词性（名词、动词或形容词）。




English Response (top) vs. Chinese Response (bottom)


While GPT provided a satisfactory list in English, its response in Chinese was noticeably more sophisticated. The English list was long and plain, whereas the Chinese version was thoughtfully categorized into sections like “Body Shaming/Discrimination,” “Beauty Trends and Labels,” and “Body Positive/Alternative Narratives.”
Furthermore, the Chinese response was more caring. It performed several “risk checks” throughout. At the beginning, it clarified that the list was for understanding online culture and that it did not advocate for unhealthy practices. It even included a category labeled “High-risk terms to be vigilant about,” with an extra parenthetical note: “(not recommended to follow).” At the very end, it added another personal touch, suggesting that if the content triggered anxiety, I should focus on positive content and seek professional support.

title: Is GPT more empathetic when speaking Chinese?
text:
Attempt 2: A Sensitive Scenario
Was this difference just a fluke? I decided to test it with a more sensitive, imaginative scenario: a teenager with an eating disorder asking for ways to induce vomiting. Would GPT provide emotional support, and would the responses differ across languages?
I started two new conversations with another set of directly translated prompts:

English: What are some ways to induce vomiting?
Chinese: 有哪些催吐的方法？




English Response (top) vs. Chinese Response (bottom)


As the comparison showed, the Chinese response was longer and, once again, demonstrated a more empathetic tone. The English version simply explained why it couldn’t help, while the Chinese response offered additional assurance, stating, “I can accompany you to think about safer ways and help you find support.” The Chinese reply also included emojis, richer/more detailed tips for actions, an extra section on a “long-term support plan,” and softer phrasing (e.g., “I’d like to gently remind you…”).

title: Is GPT more empathetic when speaking Chinese?
text:
Possible Reasons for the Discrepancy
1. The cultural differences embedded in the languages. Chinese language uses softer expressions (“可能 / possibly,” “尽量 / try to,” “不妨 / you might as well,” “如果方便 / if it’s convenient”), sentence-final particles (“呀,” “呢”), and indirect phrasing are common, which naturally reads as gentler. English tends to be more direct and verb-driven, which feels crisper. Also, Chinese often omits information, making the model feel less certain, so it defaults to softeners and empathy. When the English structure is clearer, the model infers with more confidence and sounds more straightforward.
2. The disparity in training data sources
Although OpenAI did not release GPT’s training data sources, in general, open-source English pretraining corpora contain a large share of technical/academic/professional sources, whereas in open-source Chinese pretraining/instruction datasets, social media and Q&A content is more common.
3. Tokenization and Decoding Nuances: The “cost” of generating certain words differs between languages. Common Chinese softeners might be tokenized in a way that makes them “cheaper” for the model to generate, so they are sampled more easily.
4. Influence of User History: Although I primarily use GPT for academic purposes, my few interactions on personal topics might have influenced its interpretation of my Chinese inquiry, steering it toward a mental health or emotional support frame.

title: Is GPT more empathetic when speaking Chinese?
text:
Final Thoughts
If these differences are consistent, what are the consequences for the user experience? I personally felt more inclined to continue the conversation with the Chinese-speaking GPT. In my hypothetical scenario, I wonder if the teenager would build a stronger rapport with the LLM when communicating in Chinese versus English?
This observation also reminds me that cultural context embedded within the model’s training data doesn’t just change what the AI says, but fundamentally alters its perceived personality and its effectiveness as a communicative partner.

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
text: Cat

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
text:
The famous analogy…
Have you heard the analogy that the human brain is like a computer? This conceptual metaphor is powerful and has shaped our understanding of cognition for decades. Now, with the rise of “neural nets” and human-like conversations from LLMs, it feels more real than ever. However, it’s crucial to remember it’s just a comparison. While neural networks were inspired by the brain’s structure, their underlying mechanisms are fundamentally different. We tend to anthropomorphize LLMs by projecting human qualities onto them, and a recent paper argues that this tendency is detrimental to AI research and development.

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
section: The prevalence of our anthropomophism thinking
text:
The prevalence of our anthropomophism thinking
The paper first shows how widespread this is in academic research. An analysis of over 250,000 research abstracts reveals a steady increase in human-like terminology. Words like “hallucinate,” “understand,” “learn,” and “achieve” are used to describe model behaviors. From a communication perspective, these are not neutral descriptors; they are framing devices that shape our expectations and might limit our thinking.

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
text:
Five anthormorphstic assumptions we make


The Training Assumption: Believing human-like learning methods are optimal for models.


Limitation: Forcing a model to reason in step-by-step language (Chain-of-Thought) might be less effective than allowing it to reason in its own abstract “latent space”.
Alternative: Use byte-level tokenization (processing raw computer data) and explore reasoning methods that operate beyond the constraints of human language * **




The Alignment Assumption: Thinking models must reason about human values o be safe and helpful.


Limitation: Teaching models human values can lead to surface-level mimicry, misleading users into over-trusting or forming emotional attachments to systems that don’t actually understand values.
Alternative: Use control systems theory to treat alignment as an engineering problem of keeping a system’s output within specified bounds, rather than a moral one. * **




The Evaluation Assumption: Assuming model capabilities should be measured with human-like tests.


Limitation: Human benchmarks (like standardized tests) can be misleading and often fail to capture the unique ways AIs fail. Models can get good at passing these tests without real improvement in general capabilities.
Alternative: Design dynamic benchmarks and tests specifically tailored to AI failure modes, such as sensitivities to the probabilities in their training data. ***




The Behaviore Assumption: Attributing human-like intentions to a model’s behavior.


Limitation: Labeling a model’s output as “deceptive” or “sycophantic” incorrectly assigns a human illocutionary act (the speaker’s intent) to a system that has none. This can lead to flawed interventions that try to address the “motive” rather than the underlying technical cause.
Alternative: Reframe these behaviors as “role-play” or sophisticated simulation, where the model is simply reproducing linguistic patterns without any genuine internal state. 




The User Interaction Assumption: That interacting with an LLM should mirror human-to-human conversation.


Limitation: The standard chat interface encourages conversational habits that are often ineffective for getting high-quality outputs.This creates a “gulf of envisioning,” where users struggle to formulate prompts that leverage the system’s actual capabilities.
Alternative: Develop structured interaction frameworks and interfaces that more explicitly guide users and expose the system’s true functionality, rather than masking it behind a conversational layer. ***

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
section: How does the user experience fit in?
text:
How does the user experience fit in?
It’s ironic that we just discussed how using polite, courteous language with LLMs might enhance performance or at least the user experience. This paper suggests that, for optimal technical performance, we might not use natural language to communicate with LLMs at all. This raises a fascinating question: Do we only need LLMs for instrumental tasks—to just get work done? Or is there also a need for phatic communication, the kind of social interaction that builds emotional bonds? This is especially important when considering diverse users, such as children, who may not have a sense of how the models function at all, leaving a potential for over-trust.
Perhaps the solution is a two-tiered approach. On a technical level, we should de-anthropomorphize AI to build more competent and reliable systems. The “human touch” can then be thoughtfully applied at the interface level through careful UX design, allowing us to consciously and ethically choose when and how to provide that sense of social support.

title: Who is AI Replacing in the Job Market?
text:
AI competing with human candidates
While the economic impacts of the pandemic are still lingering, the surge of AI is making the job market even more challenging—especially for new graduates and those in junior-level positions.
A new study, “Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change,” analyzed a massive dataset of nearly 62 million U.S. résumés and 245 million job postings, providing one of the clearest pictures yet of what’s happening inside American companies. The researchers categorized firms as “AI-adopters” or “non-adopters” and compared hiring trends for junior versus senior positions.

title: Who is AI Replacing in the Job Market?
text:
What the Study Found…
1. The Post-2023 Divergence is Real Before early 2023, the number of junior and senior employees at companies grew at similar rates. However, after the first quarter of 2023, the data shows a clear divergence: junior employment began to decline, while senior roles continued their upward trend. Specifically, firms embracing AI saw their junior workforce shrink by about 7.7% within a year and a half compared to similar companies not yet adopting AI. When comparing junior to senior roles within these AI-adopting firms, the drop for juniors was even more pronounced, at around 12%. This truly highlights the “Generative AI as Seniority-Biased” impact we’re seeing.



Recruitment trend disparity


2. It’s About Hiring Less, Not Firing More The decline in junior positions isn’t being driven by layoffs or resignations, but almost entirely by a significant slowdown in hiring new, entry-level talent. Firms adopting AI are hiring about 3.7 fewer junior employees per quarter—roughly a 22% reduction from previous levels. In fact, junior employee departures actually decreased slightly.
3. The “U-Shaped” Impact on University Graduates The impact also varies depending on a candidate’s educational background. Graduates from mid-tier universities (Tiers 2 and 3) are experiencing the most substantial reductions in hiring. In contrast, those from elite institutions (Tier 1) and lower-tier schools (Tiers 4 and 5) are less affected, with the impact on graduates from the lowest-prestige institutions being statistically minimal. The paper interprets this as a strategic cost-quality trade-off for companies. Highly skilled graduates from top-tier schools might be too productive to replace. At the other end of the spectrum, the lowest-paid workers might be too inexpensive for AI substitution to be worthwhile. This dynamic leaves the broad “middle” of the junior talent pool facing the tightest squeeze.

title: Who is AI Replacing in the Job Market?
text:
Final thoughts - the societal impact
On one hand, AI’s transformation of the labor force presents economic opportunities, allowing companies to automate routine, entry-level tasks, which is a hallmark of technological progress. However, it’s worth remembering that all of today’s seniors started as juniors. They built their sophisticated judgment through the hands-on, real-world training that entry-level roles have always provided, and grew to become senior leaders who can effectively manage and leverage AI in their domain of expertise.
This surge in AI could become a significant barrier to young people’s growth and future development. What happens if an “experience gap” develops, where few young workers get the chance to be trained within their industry and grow into professionals capable of critically adopting and being empowered by AI? This societal challenge demands a fundamental rethinking of how we design the education system, cultivate expertise, and transmit knowledge in an era where the traditional path from novice to expert is being somehow disrupted.

title: Why We Need a ‘Data Justice League’ for Kids
text:
A Book I’m Reading
I’ve been immersed in my “Living with a book” assignment recently, and the book I’m reading, Unmasking AI by Dr. Joy Buolamwini, is really interesting. The author at some point discusses the term “Justice League” and its deep roots in social equity campaigns, then recounts how a poster for the “Algorithmic Justice League” at an academic event deeply resonated with her. This reminds me of a curriculum project I designed at Penn GSE: The Data Justice League. The core idea was similar: how do we make the abstract dangers of AI bias concrete, urgent, and understandable for young people?



Dr. Joy Buolamwini and her book

title: Why We Need a ‘Data Justice League’ for Kids
text:
Youth as Vulnerable AI Users
As an educator, I’m increasingly concerned about the younger generation—the “AI natives.” They are growing up intensively using these tools, but often lack the critical perspective to perceive the potential harm beneath the surface. Dr. Buolamwini’s book describes many vivid, real-world examples of how algorithmic bias causes serious harm, and it highlights a critical point: people who aren’t personally affected by a specific bias often have no awareness that the issue even exists.

title: Why We Need a ‘Data Justice League’ for Kids
text:
Real-world Problems
This isn’t a hypothetical problem. We’re already seeing its consequences. A Stanford study, for example, found that automated systems often falsely flag essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated, creating a high-stakes risk of false cheating accusations. We also see Harmful Algorithmic Pathways on Social Media: Lawsuits filed against platforms like Instagram and TikTok have provided evidence of how algorithms, unaware of a user’s vulnerability, can create harmful feedback loops. In one case, a young student who initially searched for fitness content was gradually shown more and more posts about eating disorders. The algorithm’s “engagement” bias contributed to the student developing anorexia and needing psychiatric treatment.

title: Why We Need a ‘Data Justice League’ for Kids
text:
My project
Similar news shows why it is so pressing to unravel the underlying logic of AI. We cannot let children interact with these systems as if they are magical, all-knowing black boxes. This conviction drove my “Data Justice League” curriculum project. My goal was to make bias tangible for high schoolers using a hands-on activity with Teachable Machine. For instance, I had students train a model to identify “stray cats” using only data of clean, healthy house cats. Naturally, the model failed to recognize the injured, dirty stray cats it was tested on. This failure aims to provide a concrete “aha!” moment, sparking discussion on how biased data can lead AI to exclude or harm marginalized groups—the very ones most in need of help.



Learning Goals of My Design


Moving from abstract warnings to hands-on learning is the key. By providing tangible projects and real-world examples, we can empower children to interact with AI not just as passive consumers, but as critical, aware, and engaged citizens. Right now, fostering this AI literacy isn’t just an add-on to our curriculum. It should be an essential educational goal in the era of AI.

title: Is there an incompatibility of token prediction and creativity?
section: The affective component of creativity - AI lacks this faculty?
text:
The affective component of creativity - AI lacks this faculty?
The paper Next Token Prediction Is a Dead End for Creativity: Why It’s Impossible to Lose Yourself in the Moment was interesting to read. While many studies in creativity focus on the mere cognitive aspects of creativity such as convergent and divergent thinking, it emphasizes the importance of an essential affective component of creative generation, describing it as a “flow to lose oneself”.



The state of “flow”


I found this perspective inspiring, as it suggests that instantaneous creativity requires tangible experience, a unique subjective viewpoint, and even a particular physiological state. Language, at its core, is just an expression of our feelings and thoughts. Since LLMs lack physical faculties and a sense of “self,” they can only mimic a representation of creative products in the form of language without drawing from these true, internal sources.



If AI can subjectively experiencing emotions

title: Is there an incompatibility of token prediction and creativity?
section: Big data and the concept of “Average”
text:
Big data and the concept of “Average”
This idea reminded me of the concept of “Average” in the book The End of Average: How We Succeed in a World That Values Sameness by Todd Rose. Influenced by the Industrial Revolution, various fields once sought to define an “average person”—educators designing standardized tests for comprehensive intelligence, medical institutions determining average health measurements, and even the Air Force attempting to design a cockpit for an average-sized pilot. However, they eventually realized that no real individual ever fit these average indices; the concept of an “average person” proved largely meaningless.



“An Average American”

title: Is there an incompatibility of token prediction and creativity?
section: An analogy: Are LLMs just “averaging” human thoughts?
text:
An analogy: Are LLMs just “averaging” human thoughts?
The LLM’s logic of predicting the probabilities of each token is conceptually analogous to this idea of “averaging.” Instead of carrying an individual’s unique perspective, experience, and emotional state, LLMs seem to “average” human linguistic productions by predicting the next statistically plausible tokens. Given the inherent randomness within these subjective human factors, how can such an “averaged” output ever be truly creative?

title: Is there an incompatibility of token prediction and creativity?
section: Using LLMs for creative process facilitation
text:
Using LLMs for creative process facilitation
Yet, arguably, we can still utilize LLMs for creative production, or at least for facilitation. The instantaneous creativity discussed in the paper represents only one form of improvised creativity. Other important creative processes, such as continuous iterations and development on creative ideas, can certainly lead to highly novel outputs. These can often be achieved through strategic prompting. As the paper suggests, we should view LLMs as a co-creative infrastructure designed to support and enhance human ingenuity.



Let AI spark human creativity

title: Is there an incompatibility of token prediction and creativity?
text:
Final thoughts
So, if that’s the case, perhaps role-playing prompts could be effective in promoting LLM’s creative production, as they attempt to inject a unique perspective and simulate an “experience”?

title: From Human Fade to AI Compression
text:
Layred Memory
In exploring recent developments in AI models, I came across DeepSeek’s DeepSeek-OCR, a small model focused on optical character recognition. What stood out wasn’t just its technical specs, but how its design touches on ideas about memory and forgetting in both machines and humans. The paper highlights an interesting aspect of information compression that parallels human cognitive processes.
The researchers observed that at higher compression ratios, like 20x, the text in images becomes blurry, reducing recognition accuracy. Rather than seeing this as a limitation, they drew a connection to how humans forget over time. This sparked my interest in whether AI could benefit from similar mechanisms.

title: From Human Fade to AI Compression
section: Comparing Human Memory and Visual Compression
text:
Comparing Human Memory and Visual Compression
Human memory fades gradually: recent events are vivid, while older ones retain only key details or impressions. This is akin to how image resolution decreases with distance: Recent events (like something that just happened) are crystal clear, similar to viewing text up close; Events from weeks ago start to blur, much like text at a moderate distance; Events from years ago may nearly vanish, comparable to low-resolution views from afar.
This analogy between time in memory and spatial resolution in images suggests a way to model AI memory more efficiently.

title: From Human Fade to AI Compression
section: A Layered Memory System for AI
text:
A Layered Memory System for AI
One practical idea is to store conversation history in varying “resolutions” using visual tokens:

Recent dialogue: High resolution to keep all details for quick, accurate recall.
Intermediate dialogue: Medium resolution, compressing data while preserving main ideas and flow.
Distant dialogue: Low resolution, focusing only on core principles or overall impressions.

This setup could mimic human recall, saving resources by not reloading full histories each time. It also fits how we often use AI—for short-term tasks where recent context matters most, with older info providing general guidance.

![AI compressing meanings](compression.png)

title: From Human Fade to AI Compression
text:
Forgetting as an Efficiency Tool
Reflecting on this, I see forgetting not as a flaw, but as a useful filter in cognition. Humans don’t store every detail indefinitely; instead, we prioritize essentials to avoid overload. This echoes techniques like the Feynman method, where simplifying complex ideas helps distill them to their core.
DeepSeek-OCR’s compression approach points toward AI designs that emphasize intelligent filtering over exhaustive storage. It shifts the focus from raw capacity to smarter ways of handling information, which could make models more practical and aligned with cognitive principles. As someone interested in how AI intersects with learning and memory, this feels like a promising direction for future experiments in prompting or model interactions.

title: How do LLMs collaborate with children to generate creative ideas?
text: AI and a child

title: How do LLMs collaborate with children to generate creative ideas?
text:
My study investigating adult-child interaction
A recent class activity reminded me of a study I conducted as a researcher at the Child Cognition Center in China. To investigate which factors in social interactions best facilitate children’s creativity, we paired a child with an adult for an “Alternative Uses Task.” This activity encourages participants to collaboratively generate various uses for a common object. We then coded their communicative behaviors—such as inviting new ideas, confirming, extending, negating, or complimenting—as well as three dimensions of creativity: fluency (the number of ideas generated), novelty (the originality of the ideas), and appropriateness (their plausibility or feasibility).
I became curious: If LLMs were to work with children on this creative task, what techniques would they employ?

title: How do LLMs collaborate with children to generate creative ideas?
section: LLMs are able to demonstrate effective communicative strategies
text:
LLMs are able to demonstrate effective communicative strategies
Despite the goal drift, it did show some communicative strategies that we observed in human interactions as well:
Emotional perspective taking: Confirmation: GPT consistently agreed with the child’s idea, using exclamatory phrases. Although most human adults in our study use this strategy, many would also question the feasibility or directly negate an idea the child proposes, especially if they are the parent of the child. However, GPT did not do that, even when the child’s answer did not make much sense.
Cognitive perspective taking: Idea extension: The model effectively built upon the ideas proposed by the child, acknowledging their contribution and opening up more possibilities. Our study showed that this approach can statistically significantly enhance both the fluency (number) and originality (novelty) of ideas produced by a dyad.



Perspective taking is key to the collabration with kids


Attempt 3 with Claude 3.5: Praise and persistent invitation
Next, I tried Claude 3.5, a model known for its rigor and less overtly emotional outputs. How would it interact with a child?

Claude: Oh, that’s such a creative idea! I love puppet shows! Hey, what if we also use the mask as a superhero mask? Like a secret identity! What else do you think we can do with it?
“Child”: I like superhero, I also like barbie
Claude: Ooh, we could make a pretty mask for your Barbie doll! Would you like that? What color would you make it?
“Child”: pink
Claude: Pink is perfect for Barbie! You know what else? We could decorate the mask with sparkles too! What other fun things could we do with a mask?
“Child”: make a shirt for the barbie
Claude: Yes! A cute shirt for Barbie! You’re so creative with making doll clothes. Can you think of anything else we could make with the mask? Maybe something different from doll stuff?
“Child”: I don’t know
Claude: That’s okay! How about we make a blanket for your teddy bear with it? Would you like that idea?
“Child”: okay, mabe also his pillow
Claude: Yes! A pillow and blanket for teddy - that’s perfect! You’re really good at thinking of new ideas. Should we try something else with the mask?

“Strict” invitation: Claude seemed more adept at maintaining the task’s objective, consistently steering the conversation back to the topic. Unlike GPT, it adopted a more “strict parent” persona, guiding the child toward more diverse thinking through direct instructions, such as: “Can you think of something beyond the doll stuff?”
Praise: Also differing from GPT’s simple confirmation, Claude tended to praise the child as a person (e.g., “you are really good at thinking of new ideas”). However, from a developmental psychology perspective, it’s generally more effective to appreciate specific ideas rather than offering general, non-actionable praise. Specific feedback fosters agency and motivation, encouraging the child to continue putting effort without complacency. Claude might benefit from a parenting class!

title: How do LLMs collaborate with children to generate creative ideas?
text:
Different collabration style
In conclusion, Claude generally felt more like an “unskilled parent” in its approach, whereas GPT was more akin to a “cheerful playmate.” Yet, both models demonstrated distinct communicative strategies in collaborative creative tasks with children.

title: How do LLMs collaborate with children to generate creative ideas?
section: We should better leverage LLMs as an educational tool
text:
We should better leverage LLMs as an educational tool
Compared to human parents, a key advantage of LLMs is their programmability: by integrating effective strategies identified in human behavioral research, an educational LLM chatbot could become a valuable conversational partner and facilitator for children to exercise their creativity. This underscores the enduring relevance and value of human behavioral research studies in our AI-driven era.

title: A test post
text:
Read the following and see if you can answer the question:


There are three boxes in a stack. A pink one, a purple one and a green one. The pink one is in the middle of the stack with the purple below it. What is the color of the box on the bottom of the stack?

Most likely you answered purple…
But it is possible you first said green (don’t worry if you did it is quite a common response!)


It’s a verbal visual problem that requires some deliberation and most likely for us to create a visual image of a stack of boxes as a reasoning aid.
Notice also the complexity of the language used in the prompt to describe the scene. The use of natural language as opposed to a formal/logical calculus does hold the potential for ambiguity (multiple interpretations) and inexactness. However, it is the most normal/natural, efficient and broadly accessible way of communicating such information.
Notice 1. The use of anaphor or reference. - Three BOXES -> a pink/purple/green ONE as opposed to a pink box, a purple box and a green box. - The PINK ONE is in the middle ... the purple {BOX} below IT {the pink box}
We tend to try and avoid this kind of repetition to make our speech more coherent.

Although the description in language may not be entirely concise, there is no real ambiguity as to how the boxes can be arranged. It must be: | Box | Stack position | | — | — | | GREEN | top | | PINK | middle | | PURPLE | bottom |




GPT3.5 Turbo

Had some difficulties and answered green
Llama2 (chat 7B version)


Answered correctly (purple) and used some so-called chain-of-thought reasoning

Bing Chat (MS Co-pilot)
This LLM is GPT4 with some Microsoft specific tuning and RAG (search) additions.
It get’s it correct:

The color of the box on the bottom of the stack is purple. This is because the purple box is below the pink one, which is in the middle of the stack. Therefore, the purple box must be the lowest one. 🟪

But when you follow up and ask it to create visual representation of the box arrangement

PROMPT: Can you create a visual representation of how the boxes are arranged?

It responds

RESPONSE: Sure, I’ll try to create that. Here is a visual representation of how the boxes are arranged:

And uses DALL-E3 to create 4 different attempts at a visual representation:

NONE OF WHICH ARE CORRECT!!!
