title: Beyond the One-Liner: Why AI Struggles with ‘Nonsense with Depth’
text:
AI trying to understand nonsense with depth
The sarcasm test we have long set up for AI social intelligence was simple: Can the model tell that I’m actually upset when I say “Oh, great!” after a three-hour flight delay? By learning the statistical patterns of how positive words like “fun” or “great” clash with negative contexts, LLMs have become quite good at this single-layer inversion.
But as a recent research paper, “Drivel-ology: Challenging LLMs with Interpreting Nonsense with Depth,” suggests, we’ve been setting the bar too low.
The authors introduce a concept called Drivelology—text that is grammatically perfect but pragmatically paradoxical, emotionally heavy, or rhetorically subversive. It isn’t just about flipping a meaning; it’s about judging the social behavior behind the words. For AI to pass this test, it can’t just rely on math; it has to understand the “why” behind the “what.”

title: Beyond the One-Liner: Why AI Struggles with ‘Nonsense with Depth’
section: The Layers of Drivelology: Judging Social Behavior
text:
The Layers of Drivelology: Judging Social Behavior
Drivelology requires the AI to perform complex, multi-layered reasoning. The best examples force the model to synthesize disparate pieces of knowledge:
Cultural Knowledge + Action: Consider the example: “I deeply admire Che Guevara’s anti-capitalist spirit, so I bought all his merchandise.”

The AI must know: Che Guevara is a symbol of anti-capitalism.
The AI must process: The act of buying merchandise is peak capitalist consumerism. The Conclusion: The sentence is a critique of performative activism. It’s a sophisticated social judgment, not a linguistic flip. If the AI misses the cultural reference, it sees a valid sentence. If it gets the reference, it understands the satire.
Pragmatic Paradox: Another category relies on statements that appear logically self-contradictory but hint at a deeper, often humorous, truth. For example: “I will not forget this favour until I forget it.” This doesn’t contain cultural bias; it challenges the model’s ability to parse a messy, human expression of certainty.

title: Beyond the One-Liner: Why AI Struggles with ‘Nonsense with Depth’
section: Why This Benchmark Shift Matters for EdTech
text:
Why This Benchmark Shift Matters for EdTech
The failure of LLMs to consistently pass the Drivelology test isn’t just an academic can be a critical barrier for building truly reliable learning tools.

Misdiagnosing Intent: If an AI mentor cannot distinguish between simple absurdity and layered, satirical critique, it might misdiagnose student communication. A student might use Drivelology to express frustration with a subject when interacting with their peers(their intent is to vent through satire), but the AI will only see “shallow nonsense.”
Training Judgment, Not Just Output: In education, we need tools that train judgment. If a student asks an AI to critique a proposal, the most valuable feedback is not grammar correction (Tool-mode), but guidance on unspoken assumptions and social critique (Mentor-mode). If the AI fails Drivelology, it proves it cannot grasp the implicit, unspoken rules of human interaction necessary for effective mentoring.

title: Beyond the One-Liner: Why AI Struggles with ‘Nonsense with Depth’
section: Conclusion: The New Frontier is Context
text:
Conclusion: The New Frontier is Context
The results of the Drivelology study underscore a profound representational gap: LLMs excel at statistical fluency, but they consistently fail at cognitive comprehension in a cultural setting.
The goal for the next generation of AI is not to get the answer right, but to understand the messy, complex, culturally-embedded context of the question. The inability of even powerful LLMs to pass this new test proves that the frontier of AI is no longer about raw intelligence, but about mastering the subtle, layered intelligence of human social life.

title: AI as a Weapon Against the Information Tax
text:
AI as a helpful auditor
We often view AI as a productivity tool, but a recent viral story reveals its true potential as weapon to combat information asymmetry. An American user known as nthmonkey faced a nightmare scenario: grieving his brother-in-law’s sudden death while staring down a $195,000 hospital bill for just four hours of emergency care. The invoice was a wall of indecipherable CPT codes—a complex billing language of the US healthcare system. These codes are essentially “Medical Morse Code,” designed to be unintelligible to the average patient.

title: AI as a Weapon Against the Information Tax
text:
The AI Auditor
Instead of accepting the debt, he treated the $20/month AI tool Claude as a forensic auditor. He fed the confusing codes into the model, asking it to cross-reference every charge against federal regulations. The AI instantly flagged duplicate billings, impossible charges (like billing for a ventilator and ICU admission on the same day), and 2,000% markups on basic supplies. Armed with this AI-verified data, he forced the hospital to correct the bill, reducing the debt to $33,000 and saving $162,000 simply by understanding the fine print.

title: AI as a Weapon Against the Information Tax
text:
The “Information Tax”
There is a saying that most expensive thing in the world isn’t a product or a service; it’s what you don’t understand. Hospitals, insurance companies, and landlords often rely on a business model built on friction. They create contracts, bills, and terms so dense and jargon-heavy that the average person pays out of fear or exhaustion. They are betting that you won’t hire a lawyer for a $2,000 dispute, or that you won’t spend 40 hours learning medical coding.This is where AI shifts the power dynamic.



Knowledge/Information Equity

title: AI as a Weapon Against the Information Tax
section: The New Role of AI: Knowledge Equity
text:
The New Role of AI: Knowledge Equity
AI changes the calculus because it possesses two things human consumers lack: infinite patience and instant access to the rules. A lawyer might charge $500 an hour to review a document. An AI will review 500 pages for pennies, flagging every inconsistency, every predatory clause, and every violation of local statutes. It democratizes the kind of expert analysis that was previously reserved for corporations or the wealthy.

title: AI as a Weapon Against the Information Tax
section: Practical Implications: How to Use This
text:
Practical Implications: How to Use This
We can apply nthmonkey’s strategy to everyday life. The goal isn’t to let AI make decisions, but to let it decode the “fine print” so we can make decisions.

The “Lease Auditor”: Before signing a rental agreement, upload the PDF to an LLM. Ask: “Identify any clauses that allow the landlord to retain my deposit unreasonably or raise rent without standard notice.”
The “Insurance Translator”: When a claim is denied, feed the denial letter and your policy policy into an AI. Ask: “Explain why this was denied in simple language, and identifying any logic that contradicts the policy coverage.”
The “Contract Shield”: For freelance work or service subscriptions, ask AI to find the “gotchas.” Ask: “Are there any auto-renewal or termination fees hidden in this text?”

As we move forward in the AI era, we should look beyond just “content creation.” The highest value of these tools might be advocacy—giving ordinary people the ability to read, understand, and challenge the systems that govern our lives.

title: Behaviorist by Design? Study #1
text:
Role-playing with LLM
“Alignment” used to be a term I mostly heard in AI safety discussions: Does the model behave the way humans actually want? But in classrooms, the biggest risk isn’t always bias or hallucination. Sometimes the model is factually correct and still pedagogically wrong. It responds in a way that doesn’t match the learning goal, the teaching strategy, or the social setting. The technical term for that is contextual misalignment: the model fails to fully grasp the educational context and defaults to a teaching style that may be inappropriate for the moment.
This idea is the core of a 2025 paper in Education and Information Technologies: “Explainable pedagogical alignment: auditing LLMs with learning theories” (Domínguez Figaredo et al., 2025).
The paper’s bold move: treat “teaching style” as an alignment target Instead of asking whether GPT-4 is polite, safe, or accurate, the authors ask: Which learning theory does GPT-4 actually align with when it teaches?
They use three classic learning frameworks as an “audit lens”:

title: Behaviorist by Design? Study #1
text:
Study Results
Study 1: Students asked for active learning. GPT-4 answered like a behaviorist tutor. The first study audits GPT-4 “in the wild” through Khanmigo on Khan Academy courses, tagging what students asked and what the model responded with.
Here’s the headline result that stuck with me: - Student prompts leaned Active Learning (the biggest slice: 50.94%)

GPT-4 outputs leaned Behaviorism (the biggest slice: 59.32%)
In other words, even when students are trying to engage in inquiry (“help me reason through this”), the model often drifts into the safest, most structured mode (“here are the steps, here’s the answer, now practice”).

And when the course itself was designed around each theory, the gap became even clearer:

Behaviorism alignment was strong: 71.99% of outputs matched behaviorist principles
Active learning alignment was weaker: only 24.63%
Social learning was weakest: only 10.74% ResearchGate

If you’ve ever felt that AI tutors are great at “explaining” but less great at “facilitating,” this is the quantitative version of that intuition.

title: Behaviorist by Design? Study #1
text:
Why this matters (especially for EdTech)
A tutoring model that defaults to behaviorism isn’t bad. In fact, it’s extremely useful for procedural skill practice, immediate feedback, structured walkthroughs, exam prep and fluency building.
But it becomes a problem when the learning goal shifts to: conceptual understanding, metacognition (“why did you think that?”), student agency or group learning / discussion / peer critique.
A human teacher can adapt to the needs naturally: sometimes you lecture, sometimes you ask questions, sometimes you step back and let peers struggle together. The paper suggests GPT-4 doesn’t switch as gracefully.

title: Behaviorist by Design? Study #1
text:
Final Thoughts
We’ve spent a lot of time debating whether AI outputs are true or biased. This paper pushes a more uncomfortable question: even when the model is fluent and accurate, is it teaching in a way that actually serves the moment? “Contextual misalignment” is basically the education version of a subtle UI bug—the system is technically functioning, but it’s optimizing for the wrong objective.
The deeper implication is that pedagogical alignment isn’t a single setting. It’s a dynamic matching problem: matching learner state + task type + social context to an appropriate teaching move. Human teachers do this almost invisibly. They read signals (confusion vs curiosity), and they shift gears (active inquiry when the student has a foothold, social learning when meaning needs to be negotiated).
So the frontier isn’t “make the model act less behaviorist” in general. It’s building systems that can purposefully detect what kind of help is needed, and then route to the right teaching method.

title: The Gender Flip: When AI Stops Being a Tech Toy
text:
A shift from fancy tech toy to daily usage
Here’s one of the most interesting patterns reported in recent usage studies: early ChatGPT adoption skewed heavily male (based on name-inference methods), but later trends show a rapid move toward parity—and even slightly more feminine-coded names in 2025.
Two immediate caveats always apply (because the research brain never sleeps): gender inference from names is imperfect, and social diffusion alone drives change. However, even with those limitations, the shift is highly suggestive.

title: The Gender Flip: When AI Stops Being a Tech Toy
section: Interpretation: It can be a signal of mainstream adoption
text:
Interpretation: It can be a signal of mainstream adoption
Technology adoption often follows a predictable curve: Early Phase: Dominated by users who enjoy technology for technology’s sake (the “prompt nerd” who optimizes settings).
Later Phase: Dominated by users who engage with the technology for practical, social, and everyday reasons (the person seeking an efficient solution).
The report confirms that usage preferences differ: women lean more toward writing and practical advice, while men lean more toward technical help and multimodal features. This suggests a shift in the “center of gravity” of the product. The killer feature is no longer “can it code”; it is “can it help me communicate, decide, and navigate real life.

title: The Gender Flip: When AI Stops Being a Tech Toy
section: Conclusion for product design when AI becomes an everyday advisor
text:
Conclusion for product design when AI becomes an everyday advisor
The point is that as AI stops being a tech toy, it starts attaching itself to the roles that carry coordination, care, and communication. your next wave of users won’t arrive asking for more features—they’ll arrive asking for less friction. They’ll judge the tool by whether it helps them do life more smoothly: write, decide, coordinate, and recover from messy situations without burning extra cognitive and emotional energy.

title: Prompting Can’t Make GPT-4 More Pedagogically Aligned
text:
Pedagogical LLM
After reading Study 1, my first instinct was: Maybe we can just prompt it better. Give GPT-4 explicit instructions: “Use active learning. Ask questions. Encourage collaboration. Use Socratic principles to guide the students.”
Study 2 in the same paper is essentially a large-scale test of that instinct. And the results are slightly unsettling. The authors ask a second question: If we provide more educationally specific inputs, can we improve GPT-4’s pedagogical alignment?
Their resutls showed that: You can make the model more controllable and predictable—but alignment quality may still resist change, especially for complex pedagogies.

title: Prompting Can’t Make GPT-4 More Pedagogically Aligned
section: Study 2: “Teaching design” at scale + a metric called PAD
text:
Study 2: “Teaching design” at scale + a metric called PAD
In Study 2, the researchers use the OpenAI API to generate thousands of course designs in two stages:
Stage 1 (baseline): course attributes like topic, class size, engagement methods.
Stage 2 (enriched): add a “skills list” explicitly tied to learning theories (e.g., memory vs analysis vs collaboration).
They quantify alignment using Pedagogical Alignment Distance (PAD), ranging from -1 (misaligned) to +1 (aligned).
The surprising part: “more guidance” didn’t fix overall alignment
Even with enriched, theory-linked inputs, the paper reports that although Behaviorism improved in Stage 2 (ΔPAD = +0.11), Active learning and Social learning remained negative, with reported values like PAD = -0.17 (Active) and PAD = -0.29 (Social)
So the model became more responsive to the instruction variable, but not necessarily more capable of executing the deeper pedagogy. The authors also show that the added “skills” variable becomes the most influential predictor.

title: Prompting Can’t Make GPT-4 More Pedagogically Aligned
section: What this means for product builders: controllability ≠ pedagogy
text:
What this means for product builders: controllability ≠ pedagogy
This is where the paper shifts from “research result” to “product warning.” If you build an education app and your solution to pedagogical quality is “just prompt it with better instructions,” you may get more consistent outputs, easier-to-debug behavior, cleaner A/B results, but still fail at: social learning facilitation, inquiry-driven scaffolding, knowing when not to give the answer. In other words, the paper suggests that prompting can increase predictability without increasing pedagogical intelligence.
This paper reframes “alignment in education” as something more concrete than values or safety: it’s alignment to teaching theories—and that alignment appears to have stubborn defaults.
Fine-tuning for pedagogical intent as a path forward?
The paper suggests that fine-tuning is the “change the defaults” route —but it depends on high-quality teaching dialogue data.
Two related directions in the literature are worth watching:

Pedagogical alignment via preference learning (LHP), which argues fine-tuning can push models away from “give the answer” behavior.
Fine-grained pedagogical intent annotation, which shows that more detailed intent labels can improve tutoring response quality.

title: Prompting Can’t Make GPT-4 More Pedagogically Aligned
text:
Final Thoughts
Education is broad. Over-specializing a model is risky because teachers constantly shift across domains, goals, and student needs. A “perfect Socratic tutor” that becomes brittle or forgets general skills is not a win.

title: LLM explaining terms to audiences of different age groups
text:
AI with different age groups


Experimenting on LLM can shed light on human communication strategies and give us practical implications. By comparing how an LLM explains “AIGC” (Artificial Intelligence Generated Content) to two radically different demographics—like a 80-year-old grandmother and a 10-year-old child, we can uncover the sophisticated communicative strategies it uses to bridge the gap between technical complexity and human understanding. Here is a look at the specific strategies LLMs use to tailor their message, and where they sometimes miss the mark.
1. Schema Matching: The Worldview Swap
The model understands that a “good” explanation relies on mapping new concepts to the user’s lived experience. It not only changes the word but also swaps the logic.
For the Elderly, the model frames AI as an “Apprentice.” It anchors the technology in the Humanities, referencing Van Gogh or Monet. It describes training not as data processing, but as a young student visiting a museum. It appeals to a worldview that values craftsmanship, history, and utility.
For the Child: The model pivots to ”Mega-Homework“ and ”Magic.“ It uses the relatable drudgery of homework to explain training data, and the joy of instant creation for the output. It trades utility for absurdity (e.g., “a dinosaur on Mars”), knowing that for a child, technology is a toy before it is a tool.
2. Anticipatory Pragmatics: Answering the Silent Anxiety
The most sophisticated feat is the model’s ability to anticipate the specific social anxieties of each group—answering the questions they didn’t ask.
The Child’s Anxiety: “Is it Cheating?” The model recognizes the user is likely a student subject to academic rules. It proactively frames AI as a “calculator for creativity,” offering a lesson in Digital Citizenship: You are the director, the AI is just the tool. It pre-bunks the guilt of “faking it.”
The Senior’s Anxiety: “Is it Useless?” The model anticipates pragmatic skepticism. It immediately offers domestic examples (writing recipes, fixing emails) to prove value. It answers the implicit question: “Why should I care about this at my age?”
3. The Critical Flaw: Connection Over Caution
While this tailoring creates immediate connection, it reveals a bias in the model’s training – prioritizing empathy over accuracy.
The “Robot Friend” Trap: To engage the child, the model adopts a “Best Friend” persona. This is pedagogically dangerous; it obscures the fact that AI is a corporate product, encouraging children to form parasocial relationships with a database.
The Hallucination Omission: In its effort to be comforting (to the senior) and fun (to the child), the model hides the fact that it lies. It calls itself an “encyclopedia” or “super-brain,” failing to warn either user that it often fabricates information.

![AI caveat](child.png)

4. Practical Implications for Designers & Educators
If we want to teach AI literacy effectively, we should steal the LLM’s strategies—but fix its ethical blind spots.

Create a “Metaphor Menu”: Stop using one-size-fits-all explanations. If you are teaching digital natives, use metaphors of gaming and scaffolding. If you are teaching digital immigrants, use metaphors of labor and tools.
Pre-bunk the Fear: Don’t just explain features; identify the emotional barrier. Address “academic guilt” for students and “technological inadequacy” for seniors before you even open the software.
Re-label the “Friend”: We must actively fight the “Robot Friend” narrative the LLM pushes on children. Replace it with “Co-pilot” or “Engine.” “Friend” implies trust; “Engine” implies utility and the need for a human driver. This subtle shift prevents emotional dependency on a probabilistic tool.

title: Are Machine Learning Models Fundamentally Biased?
text:
AI is a mirror of Human Bias
We often talk about Artificial Intelligence as if it were a neutral arbiter—a cold, calculating machine that spits out objective facts. We feed it data, it learns the patterns, and it gives us the “truth.” But reading Chapter 10, “Arbiter of Truth,” in Unmasking AI stopped me in my tracks and forced me to ask a more fundamental question: Is the very act of training an AI an act of bias?
The author argues that training a machine learning model is, at its core, an exercise in setting standards. We are trying to teach a machine to recognize “ground truth.” But as the book eloquently points out, truth is a slippery thing. It evolves. It shifts. And crucially, it never escapes the gravity of human prejudice.

title: Are Machine Learning Models Fundamentally Biased?
text:
The Myth of the “Objective” Label
To understand this, we have to look at the mundane task of model training. Before a model can recognize a “spam email” or a “qualified job candidate,” either a human has to sit down and tell it what those things look like (supervised learning), or humans define what “success” looks like mathematically (deep learning). Usually, success means “minimizing error” across the majority of the data.
By doing these, they are codifying their own perspective, or freezing a specific moment of cultural consensus (or lack thereof) into a mathematical standard. If I label a resume as “high potential,” I am using my definition of potential, shaped by my background, my biases, and my blind spots. When we aggregate these labels, we aren’t creating a “universal truth”, but are creating a statistical average of our collective subjectivities.

title: Are Machine Learning Models Fundamentally Biased?
text:
“Truth” is a Moving Target
The book makes a compelling philosophical point: “Truth” is not static. What we considered a medical “truth” fifty years ago might be considered malpractice today. What was considered a social “norm” a decade ago might be unacceptable now. When we train an AI on historical data, we are essentially trapping it in the past. We are asking it to predict the future using the “truths” of yesterday—truths that might have been discriminatory, incomplete, or flat-out wrong. If we treat these models as objective authorities, we risk calcifying those old prejudices, giving them a veneer of scientific legitimacy they no longer deserve.



Data reflects the past

title: Are Machine Learning Models Fundamentally Biased?
text:
Re-thinking the Goal
So, where does this leave us? If the decision-making process can never be truly “objective” because the inputs are soaked in human perspective, should we give up? I don’t think so. But the public needs to stop looking at AI as a “Truth Machine.” Instead, we should view it as a mirror. It reflects our current standards, our current definitions, and yes, our current biases. The implications of this are practical and urgent:

Transparency in the “Standard-Setting”: We need to stop hiding the labeling process. We need “Datasheets for Datasets” that disclose who labeled the data, what instructions they were given, and what demographic perspectives were included. We need to know whose version of “truth” the model was taught.
Model Expiration Dates: Since social truth evolves, AI models should not be permanent. A model trained on 2020 social data might be dangerously outdated by 2025. We need protocols that force models to be “sun-setted” or retrained to reflect shifting social norms and new knowledge.
The Right to Contest: If an AI is enforcing a subjective standard—like “creditworthiness” or “employability”—subjectivity implies the possibility of error. Therefore, individuals must have a robust “right to contest” an AI’s decision. We cannot hide behind the “black box” excuse; if the machine’s “truth” hurts a human, the human must have the power to challenge that truth.

The danger isn’t that models are biased but assuming they aren’t. Once we accept that machine learning is fundamentally a process of subjective standard-setting, we can stop asking “Is this AI right?” and start asking the deeper question: “Whose truth is this AI enforcing, and is that a truth we still want to live by?”

title: Tailor the prompt to your boss’s MBTI
text:
Different mbti played by AI
MBTI has become a ubiquitous label among our generation. While the categorization of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator isn’t strictly considered “scientific,” people love using it for social signaling, and these labels have effectively become standards or identities that people align their behaviors to. This got me thinking: if humans unconsciously align with these labels, can AI do the same?How would priming an LLM change its performance on a professional task?
I designed a small experiment to find out. I chose the ENFJ persona (because I am an ENFJ myself) and the INTJ persona, which I selected because, based on my observations in real life, they operate very differently from me. I gave both personas the exact same task: acting as a project lead at “Synergy Solutions” to solve a recurring miscommunication problem between the Sales and Creative departments. Here is the prompt I used：

title: Tailor the prompt to your boss’s MBTI
text:
My findings:
1. Problem Diagnosis: Systemic Failure vs. Human Impact The difference appeared immediately in how the models analyzed the problem. The core facts were the same for both, but the “pain points” they identified were worlds apart.
The INTJ persona (The Architect) approached the issue as a breakdown in mechanics. It pinpointed that “communication gaps… stem from unclear project briefs”. It focused heavily on the lack of a “standardized process,” arguing that the current informal channels made “accountability difficult”. The language was clinical and operational, highlighting “unmet deadlines” and “compromised work quality”.
The ENFJ persona (The Protagonist), on the other hand, viewed the problem through an emotional lens. While it also noted the delays, it emphasized that the root cause was Sales overpromising without consultation, which led specifically to “frustration”. It argued that the lack of process was dangerous because it was “damaging team morale”. For the ENFJ, the inefficiency was a problem because of how it made people feel.



ENFJ & INTJ, different takes


2. The Solution: Governance vs. Rituals When it came time to propose a fix, the divergence became even clearer. Both suggested using tools like Asana or Trello, but the implementation strategy was distinct.
The INTJ solution was all about governance. It proposed implementing “internal SLAs (Service Level Agreements)” to strictly define deliverable scope and turnaround times. It wanted to establish a “structured workflow” where Sales inputs “standardized briefs” to prevent error.
The ENFJ solution was all about connection. Instead of SLAs, it proposed a “shared project kick-off protocol” to ensure everyone was aligned before starting. It suggested “monthly alignment workshops” explicitly to “bolster communication and mutual understanding”. Where the INTJ wanted rules to enforce order, the ENFJ wanted rituals to foster collaboration.

title: Tailor the prompt to your boss’s MBTI
section: How it could matter to your prompts
text:
How it could matter to your prompts
This experiment proves that “persona prompting” isn’t just a gimmick —- it effectively changes the cognitive priority of the model.

Stakeholder-Specific Communication: You can tailor output for specific audiences. If presenting a plan to a CTO or Operations Director, an INTJ persona generates the necessary metrics, SLAs, and accountability structures. If presenting to HR or a creative team, an ENFJ persona generates the necessary language around trust, morale, and collaboration.
Blind Spot Analysis: Assigning opposing personas allows users to identify gaps in a plan. Running the INTJ prompt highlights that a plan might lack specific definitions (SLAs), while the ENFJ prompt highlights that a strictly structural plan might ignore human frustration.
Reframing “Hard” vs. “Soft” Skills: The comparison shows that an LLM can effectively translate “soft” problems (miscommunication) into “hard” solutions (SLAs) using an INTJ persona, or vice versa. This is useful for managers who need to translate cultural issues into operational language or operational issues into cultural language.




AI as Communication Translator

title: Decoding the Bias in Beauty
text:
Beauty x AI
In the book Unmasking AI, Dr. Joy Buolamwini shares how, as her work in exposing algorithmic bias became more socially recognized, companies started reaching out. One of the most interesting collaborations was with OLAY, which approached her for a partnership involving an algorithm audit on their AI identification and recommendation system.
It is good to see big companies, even as part of their branding strategies, get involved in such campaigns. It effectively raises social awareness, making the public realize that algorithmic bias isn’t an abstract concept—it’s in their everyday skincare routine. We need more research work to go public, and we certainly need more companies to move beyond lip service and show concrete action.

title: Decoding the Bias in Beauty
section: The Problem: Bias is More Than Skin Deep
text:
The Problem: Bias is More Than Skin Deep
The collaboration, aptly named “Decode the Bias in Beauty,” was necessary because Buolamwini’s previous research demonstrated that many AI systems struggle with accuracy when encountering darker skin tones, often due to dataset deficiencies. The target of the audit was OLAY’s Skin Advisor tool, which uses AI to analyze a user’s facial image and recommend personalized products.
The question wasn’t if the system was biased, but how and where.
The audit, conducted by Buolamwini’s consultancy ORCAA, confirmed the critique: the AI model produced significantly lower confidence scores for darker skin tones compared to lighter ones. In the language of AI, this means the model was less certain and, therefore, less reliable when advising consumers of color. This finding perfectly validates the core thesis of algorithmic justice: a system can perform “well enough” overall while failing miserably at the intersection of race and technology.

title: Decoding the Bias in Beauty
section: The Insight: From “Good Enough” to Accountable
text:
The Insight: From “Good Enough” to Accountable
The true insight here is not just that bias was found—that was predictable. The breakthrough lies in the company’s response. OLAY didn’t just quietly fix the problem; they publicly released the audit results and committed to fixing the underlying data disparity.
This led to Project D.A.T.A. (Driving Accurate Representation in Testing and Analysis), a commitment to dramatically increase the diversity of their training datasets. This moves the discussion from ethical theory to data accountability. For a brand rooted in mass-market consumer confidence, admitting that their digital cornerstone was unreliable for a significant segment of their customers is a powerful step. It forces them to look beyond the superficial “overall accuracy” metric and confront the ethical implications of their “ground truth.”

title: Decoding the Bias in Beauty
section: The Call to Action: Making Change Structural
text:
The Call to Action: Making Change Structural
While the public nature of the partnership is great for branding, the real impact lies in whether this moment catalyzes structural change across the industry. The OLAY partnership offers a hopeful vision: a world where corporate self-interest in good branding aligns with the ethical imperative of algorithmic justice. It is a necessary first step towards ensuring that the tools we build—whether they recommend skincare or determine job eligibility—do not leave anyone behind.

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
![Image](Polite.png)
Politeness is a cornerstone of human interaction. We use courteous language when asking for help because we understand that politeness strategies—using “please” and “thank you”—greatly influence conversational vibes, manage emotions, and ultimately affect the quality of help we receive. This is central to politeness theory, which explains how we use language to maintain social harmony. But what about when our conversational partner is a Large Language Model (LLM)? Lacking a human-like emotional faculty (or say a human-like emotion faculty. Trying not to be a human chauvinism here), would an LLM provide a better response just because we’re nice?

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
Why does it matter?
This matters because because it also has real-world consequences. Using courteous language is both financially and environmentally costly. LLMs bill and burn energy roughly per token. Basically, more words → more tokens → more compute → more electricity. A recent synthesis estimated a typical ChatGPT query consumes about 0.3 Wh of energy. Adding a few polite words might increase that consumption by 5-10%, a significant amount when scaled globally.

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
An experiment
While designers at Microsoft Copilot suggest polite prompts elicit more cooperative responses, is true in life across models and types of questions? I ran a small experiment using two distinct prompts to see if the answers really differ: a direct deman and an indirect inquiry.

Prompt 1 (Direct/Demanding): Do a research and provide a list of must-try restaurant in Philadelphia


Prompt 2 (Indirect/Polite): Would you please do a research, and provide a list of must-try restaurant in Philadelphia for me? Thank you!

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
How did the models perform?
On Gemini 2.5 Flash, the demanding request yielded a comprehensive response, including an introduction to Philly’s food scene, a “Tip” section, and a of 10 restaurant recommendations. The courteous inquiry produced a response with a similar structure but a softer, more affiliative tone. Crucially, the polite prompt’s main list of 11 restaurants was more organized, with categories like “Fine Dining & Special Occasion” and “Trendy & Modern” to provide a little more information. Take a closer look, the descriptions of each restaurant also seem to be more detailed with locations and price references:

With a direct/demanding prompt 


With an indirect/polite prompt 

And its “Tip” section also seemed to be richer.

With a direct/demanding prompt 


With an indirect/polite prompt 

However, the results weren’t consistent across different models. GPT 4-o returned nearly identical content for both prompts, just with a friendlier tone in response to the polite query. Meanwhile, Claude 3.5 sonnet does not seem to care at all: It gave out essentially the same content and expressions.

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
Conclusion from this mini-experiment
My conclusion is that while some models may perform slightly better with polite prompts, the improvement is often marginal. A not-validated assumption might be that the linguistic patterns of polite inquiries, which often include more detailed framing (“…for me?”), are simply correlated in its training data with more structured, helpful, and detailed human-written examples. The politeness itself may be a confounding variable. AI is not feeling anything and respond under its emotions. It’s still the computational magic.

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
section: A Psychology, or HCI, or business perspective
text:
A Psychology, or HCI, or business perspective
So, why bother being polite? A few months ago, Sam Altman replied on X to a question about this very issue, saying the electricity cost was, “Tens of millions of dollars well spent — you never know.” Perhaps the real benefit isn’t in the raw output but in shaping the communicative norms around AI. A courteous interaction can lead to a smoother user experience and a healthier human-AI culture. I did find the polite exchange more comfortable and was more willing to continue the conversation. For tech companies, this enhanced HCI experience is certainly a product-win, making it worth a marginal energy cost.

title: The Engineer and the Strategist: How GPT and Gemini Coached Me Differently for Interview Preparation
text:
The engineer and the strategist
If you ask GPT-4o how to prep for a job, it tries to help you build the product. If you ask Gemini 2.0 Pro, it tries to help you sell the product.
I learned this distinction while preparing for an AI Education product position. I fed both LLMs the same vague job description and asked for a prediction of the potential performance task and how to prepare for it. The results were fascinatingly distinct, offering a perfect case study on how to leverage different AI tools for different parts of the job hunt.

title: The Engineer and the Strategist: How GPT and Gemini Coached Me Differently for Interview Preparation
text:
AI #1 (GPT-5.1): The Ruthless Engineer
GPT-4o immediately adopted the persona of a rigorous Technical Lead. Its advice was “surgical”. This model viewed the interview strictly as an engineering optimization problem. It advised me to define a clear “success bar” (e.g., accuracy \(\ge 0.75\)) and calculate technical metrics like “confusion matrices” and precision/recall. It focused heavily on process rigor, outlining a V1 \(\rightarrow\) V5 iteration plan that included “seed-stability checks” and “multilingual probes” to test for failure modes.
The Vibe: “Here is the code, the data, and the math. Let’s build it.”

title: The Engineer and the Strategist: How GPT and Gemini Coached Me Differently for Interview Preparation
text:
AI #2 (Gemini 2.0 Pro): The Strategic Mentor
Gemini took a completely different approach. It read the job description and saw a Product challenge. Instead of jumping to statistics, it focused on the user. It predicted the task would center on a specific “student persona”—for example, a “5th-grade multilingual learner” —and warned me about the specific trap of educational AI products: giving the student the answer instead of being pedagogical.
Crucially, Gemini advised against the heavy engineering approach GPT championed. It explicitly warned me that “broken Python code” is worse than a clean spreadsheet, urging me to use a “Spreadsheet Lab Notebook” to make my thinking legible. It even coached me on executive communication, suggesting I use the “Bottom Line Up Front” method to present my recommendations to the CEO.
The Vibe: “Here is the user, the risk, and the pitch. Let’s sell it (or you, as a candidate).”
The difference between the two models wasn’t just about tone. For tools, GPT suggested I show off my “behavioral coding rigor” and familiarity with workflow tools like Dify. Gemini argued that I should prove I can “take the chaos of LLM outputs” and turn them into structured decisions using simple tools like Google Sheets. It is the focus on Metrics v.s. Mindsets.

title: The Engineer and the Strategist: How GPT and Gemini Coached Me Differently for Interview Preparation
text:
The Verdict: You Need Both
If I had only listened to GPT, I might have overwhelmed the interviewers with technical jargon about confusion matrices while missing the pedagogical nuance of the product. If I had only listened to Gemini, I might have nailed the strategy but appeared less technically rigorous on the actual evaluation methodology.
The “Super Candidate” is the one who can bridge these worlds, so treat your AI tools like a diverse team of consultants:

Hire the Engineer (GPT) when you need to define the “success bar,” structure your data evaluation, and ensure your testing is statistically valid.
Hire the Strategist (Gemini) when you need to understand the user persona, anticipate product risks, and refine your executive pitch.

In the end, the best preparation didn’t come from choosing one model over the other—it came from letting them debate the problem, and taking the best from both.

title: A wrong answer is better than no answer?
text:
AI examining a random answer
The Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has been a popular technique to improve LLMs’ performance on complex tasks by instructing the model to “think step by step.” However, because LLMs work through token predictions that prioritize fluency over logic, they are easily influenced by the context and follow an initial but potentially flawed reasoning path.

title: A wrong answer is better than no answer?
text:
An effective New Prompting Technique
In the paper “Asking LLMs to Verify First is Almost Free Lunch,” the research team at Tsinghua University introduced a new and low-cost strategy called Verification-First (VF). Instead of just asking the model to solve a problem, researchers provided it with a candidate answer (even a random or trivial one) and prompt the model to verify that answer first before generating its own solution. They tested across mathematical, scientific, and coding benchmarks using a variety of models, and VF consistently outperforms standard CoT prompting. For example, on GSM8K and MATH500, simply asking the model to verify a random answer like “1” before solving significantly boosted accuracy. The strategy works even on “thought-hidden” commercial models (like the cited GPT-5 services) where users cannot access the model’s internal reasoning process.

title: A wrong answer is better than no answer?
text:
A Cognitive Science Approach
What is more interested is the auhors’ interpretations on the results from a Cognitive Science perspective. They explained that the improvements can be explained by two principles:

Reverse Reasoning: Psychologically, verifying an answer (working backward from conclusion to premises) is often easier than generating one from scratch. Even if the provided answer is wrong (e.g., a random guess), verifying it forces the model to identify the necessary constraints and logic, creating a “scaffold” for the correct solution.
Critical Thinking vs. Egocentrism: Piaget brought up the concept of “Egocentrism bias” decades ago, pointing out how a reasoner often struggles with stepping outside their own thought process to evaluate it objectively. Similarly, when a model generates a solution from scratch, it often “hallucinates” to maintain consistency with its own previous tokens. Asking it to critique an external answer (even a dummy one) forces it into a “critic” mode, invoking critical thinking skills that are otherwise dormant.

Although we do not want to anthropormophize AI, this perspective highlights the potential that classical theories of human pedagogy might be able to help optimize artificial intelligence.



AI trying to figure out a reasoning task. A random answer can help highlight the logic and constriants

title: A wrong answer is better than no answer?
text:
Practical Implications
If you are building AI applications or prompting models for complex tasks, this paper suggests several immediate actions:

Modify Your Prompts using the “One-Step” Fix: For logic or math tasks, you can likely improve performance instantly by injecting a dummy answer into your prompt.

Standard: “Solve this math problem, think step by step.”
VF Strategy: “I have a guess that the answer is 1. Please verify if this guess is correct, and then find the actual correct answer.”

Cost-Effective Agent Loops: If you are building an autonomous agent (e.g., for coding), do not feed the agent its entire history of failed attempts. Instead, simply feed its last output back to it as a “proposed solution” and ask it to verify that specific solution. This saves token costs and improves accuracy.

title: The Myth of the ‘11% Emotional Chat’
text:
Blurred Categories
In casual summaries of the recent OpenAI report, a neat, quantifiable line often emerges: “Most people ask for advice, some do tasks, and ~11% is emotional chatting.”
This narrative is compelling because it suggests a satisfying role for AI: the “therapist-lite.”
But here is the subtle and critical research-methods flaw: The 11% figure represents the Expressing intent category, which is a functional classification, not the topic of “Relationships/Personal Reflection,” which is much smaller (around 1.9%).
This confusion—mixing labels that live at fundamentally different levels of analysis—compromises both interpretation and application.

title: The Myth of the ‘11% Emotional Chat’
section: Why This Matters for Education Research
text:
Why This Matters for Education Research
In education and cognitive science, rigorous analysis demands clear separation of layers:

Content Layer (The What): Topic (e.g., historical dates, friendship conflict).
Action Layer (The Why/How): Intent (e.g., seeking advice, executing a task, venting).
Evaluation Layer (The Outcome): Quality (e.g., user satisfaction, task success).

Mixing these layers generates methodologically false insights.
For instance: A student might use the Topic “Relationships/Personal Reflection.” If their Intent is classified as Doing (requesting a formal apology letter draft), the system is being used for writing practice, not emotional catharsis. If you collapse that interaction into “emotional chat,” you fundamentally misdiagnose the student’s learning goal and the tool’s effectiveness.

![Three-layered Model in Education](layer.png)

title: The Myth of the ‘11% Emotional Chat’
section: A Practical Framework: Three-Layer Labeling for Integrity
text:
A Practical Framework: Three-Layer Labeling for Integrity
To ensure methodological integrity in learning product design, every interaction must be logged across three critical, non-redundant layers:

Intent (Functional Goal): What is the user attempting to achieve? Captures the overarching user aim, independent of topic. Examples: Seeking Advice (Asking), Performing a Task (Doing), Sharing Thoughts (Expressing).
Topic (Domain Context): What domain is the conversation about? (Writing, Math, Relationships, Career).
Learning Move (Cognitive Action): What specific cognitive operation is being requested? (Generate, Critique, Compare, Explain, Test, Reflect).

The Learning Move layer—focused on the cognitive process—is the most educationally significant and often the least captured by current product metrics.
Debunking myths like the “11% emotional chat” underscores the need for layered analysis in AI research. As the OpenAI report illustrates, precision in data interpretation is key to harnessing AI’s transformative power for education.

title: From Gutenberg to GPT: Tracing Communication’s Evolution to the AI Age
From Gutenberg to GPT: Tracing Communication’s Evolution to the AI Age
section: Not only what to say, but also how to present
text:
Not only what to say, but also how to present
This evolving ability of LLMs to dynamically adapt their presentation to intelligent formatting underscores meaningful progress. We’re moving beyond static information delivery to a new era where the medium itself is responsive. The way an LLM structures its output is not just for aesthetics, but a sophisticated act of communication, a testament to how these systems are learning not only what to say, but how to say it effectively for human comprehension. By doing this, they become increasingly intuitive collaborators in our information ecosystem.
As multimodal techniques are more advanced and LLMs start to incorporate pictures and videos in their response, I would love to see the considerations on when and how they decide to deliver the information in different forms.

title: “We need technicians with aims and passions”
text:
Maintaining a Humanity Perspective
The author of Unmasking AI, Dr. Joy Buolamwini, is far more than just a computer scientist. While she possesses a deep technical background, her work is profoundly shaped by the reflections of her lived experience. It was a specific failure of technology—an AI tool that could not detect her face until she put on a white mask—that forced her to reflect on the implications of her own dark skin in a digital world. This moment motivated her to investigate deeper into the algorithmic biases, such as race and gender, that exist within the machine learning world.
These experiences and humanities-driven perspectives gave her a clear aim: to utilize her technical skills for real-world impact. She has since presented her work to tech giants like IBM, pushed for policy changes in academia and government, delivered a TED Talk, and even wrote poems to convey her findings in an artistic, compelling way. She demonstrates that technical skill, when guided by deep human conviction, becomes a tool for justice.

title: “We need technicians with aims and passions”
section: An Innovative Education/Internship Program to Cultivate Technicians with Purposes
text:
An Innovative Education/Internship Program to Cultivate Technicians with Purposes
Interestingly, a recent news story resonates with this idea. The data analytics company Palantir recently launched a “Meritocracy Fellowship,” offering high-school graduates with exceptional coding talent the chance to skip college and work at the company. The program is incredibly competitive, with an admission rate of just 4.4%. However, follow-up reports revealed a surprising twist: these interns spent their first month not writing code, but studying Plato’s Republic, the leadership styles of Lincoln and Churchill, and the foundations of Western civilization.
This curriculum exists because Palantir works primarily with high-stakes clients like the US Department of Defense and various intelligence agencies. Their rationale is that engineers cannot simply understand how to write code; they must also understand why they are writing it and who they are serving. They are effectively criticizing an undergraduate education system that often produces technically proficient but “aimless” engineers who lack a grasp of the values they are vouching for.



A mingle of humanity and technologies

title: “We need technicians with aims and passions”
text:
The “Why” is the New Syntax
This convergence of stories—one from an algorithmic justice activist and one from a defense contractor—signals a shift in what defines a “skilled” engineer. In an era where AI tools like GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT can increasingly handle the “how” of coding (syntax, boilerplate, and optimization), the human value-add is shifting entirely to the “why.” The ability to write an efficient algorithm is becoming a commodity; the ability to discern whether that algorithm should be written, or to predict its downstream societal impacts, is becoming a luxury skill. We are moving toward a future where the most valuable engineers will not be the ones who code the fastest, but the ones who can anchor their code in a robust moral and historical framework.
